title: Open repair of ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm
subtitle: Outline level, with damage control

sources.title: ESVS 2024 Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Management of Abdominal Aorto-Iliac Artery Aneurysms
The Society for Vascular Surgery practice guidelines on the care of patients with an abdominal aortic aneurysm

indications: Ruptured or symptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm when anatomy is unsuitable for endovascular repair or an endovascular service is not available in time.
Failed or complicated endovascular repair needing conversion.
Rupture with a hostile aortic neck, a juxtarenal aneurysm, or iliac anatomy that will not take a stent graft.
contraindications: A patient who has declined surgery or in whom repair is judged futile after senior discussion with the patient or family.
A patient whose anatomy and the local service make emergency EVAR the faster and safer option.
preparation: Consultant vascular surgeon and consultant anaesthetist present; major haemorrhage protocol active, cell salvage set up, blood in theatre.
Arterial line and large-bore access placed in theatre, without delaying the start.
Grafts of several sizes, straight and bifurcated, open and checked before induction.
Plan for proximal control: supracoeliac clamp, infrarenal clamp, or an aortic occlusion balloon via the femoral or brachial route.
positioning: Supine, arms out, with a warming blanket below the waist and fluid warmers on every line.
Urinary catheter and nasogastric tube after induction if not already in place.
equipment: Major vascular tray with aortic clamps of several angles, iliac clamps and a self-retaining retractor.
Tube and bifurcated grafts; polypropylene sutures; pledgets.
Cell salvage, rapid infuser, and an aortic occlusion balloon with a sheath ready.
Materials for temporary abdominal closure if the abdomen cannot be closed.
anatomy: The left renal vein crosses anterior to the aorta at the neck and is the landmark for an infrarenal clamp. It may be retro-aortic or circumaortic.
The inferior mesenteric artery arises from the front of the sac; the lumbar arteries arise from its back and bleed into the open sac.
The iliac veins lie behind and lateral to the iliac arteries and are easily torn by circumferential dissection.
The left ureter crosses the left iliac bifurcation; the duodenum lies over the neck of the aneurysm.
Supracoeliac control is gained through the lesser omentum, by dividing the crura of the diaphragm onto the aorta.
criticalSafety: Prepare and drape before induction. Induction can drop the pressure catastrophically, and the knife must be ready.
Proximal control is the operation. Clamp first, dissect later.
Do not dissect the iliac arteries circumferentially. Clamp from the front or use balloon catheters from inside.
Measure intra-abdominal pressure after repair and do not force the abdomen closed.
structuresAtRisk: Iliac veins and the inferior vena cava
Inferior mesenteric artery and the left colon
Superior mesenteric artery and renal arteries with a high clamp
commonErrors: Induction before the surgeon is scrubbed and the abdomen draped.
Searching for an infrarenal neck in a large haematoma instead of clamping above the coeliac axis and moving the clamp down later.
Tearing the iliac veins during circumferential iliac dissection.
Closing a tense abdomen and causing abdominal compartment syndrome.
complications: Death: mortality remains high, and most deaths are from haemorrhage, cardiac events and multi-organ failure.
Colonic ischaemia, typically of the left colon, presenting with diarrhoea, blood or acidosis.
Acute kidney injury, particularly after a suprarenal clamp or prolonged hypotension.
Myocardial infarction, respiratory failure and coagulopathy.
postop: Critical care with monitoring of bladder pressure, lactate, urine output and limb perfusion.
Low threshold for sigmoidoscopy for suspected colonic ischaemia.
Correct coagulopathy and hypothermia; plan a return to theatre for a temporary abdominal closure.
Secondary prevention: antiplatelet therapy, statin and smoking cessation.

steps.emphasis: Consent is often a brief conversation with a shocked patient or family. Discuss the high risk of death, an open abdomen and critical care, and document it. Respect a decision not to proceed.
Keep it short but do it: blood availability, cell salvage, graft sizes and the proximal control plan are stated before induction.
Supine with arms out and warming beneath the patient. Lines are placed while the surgeon preps, not before.
Prepare and drape from the nipples to the knees, including both groins, BEFORE induction, with the surgeon scrubbed and the knife ready.
Xiphisternum to pubis, fast. Speed matters more than elegance here.
Iliac control from the front, or with balloon catheters from inside the sac. Avoid circumferential iliac dissection.
Systemic heparin is commonly reduced or omitted in rupture. Decide explicitly with the anaesthetist.
Release one iliac limb at a time after a long clamp, with the anaesthetist ready.
Check both legs and the colour of the sigmoid colon before closing.
Packs left deliberately in an open abdomen are counted and recorded as retained.
Only if it can be done without tension. Otherwise temporary abdominal closure.

step.raaa.induction.title: Induction with the surgeon scrubbed
step.raaa.induction.why: Loss of sympathetic tone and abdominal wall tone at induction can turn a contained rupture into a free one. The surgeon must be able to open and clamp within a minute of induction.
how: Confirm the surgeon is scrubbed, the abdomen prepped and draped, and suction and clamps on the table.
Anaesthetist induces with blood running and vasopressors ready.
If the patient collapses at induction, open immediately and gain proximal control by compression or a supracoeliac clamp.
pitfalls: Waiting for a central line before the abdomen is draped.

step.raaa.proximal-control.title: Proximal aortic control
step.raaa.proximal-control.why: Survival depends on how quickly the bleeding stops. Supracoeliac control is fast and safe when the neck is hidden by haematoma; the clamp can be moved below the renals once the neck is found.
how: In free rupture or a massive haematoma, compress the aorta at the hiatus or clamp above the coeliac axis through the lesser omentum after dividing the crura.
Alternatively, place an aortic occlusion balloon via the femoral or brachial route, or directly through the sac.
Then open the retroperitoneum to the left of the duodenum, find the left renal vein and place the clamp on the neck just below it.
Move the clamp down from the supracoeliac position as soon as infrarenal control is secure, and record the suprarenal clamp time.
pitfalls: Digging blindly into the haematoma looking for the neck.
Leaving a supracoeliac clamp on longer than needed, causing visceral and renal ischaemia.

step.raaa.open-sac.title: Opening the sac and controlling back-bleeding
step.raaa.open-sac.why: Lumbar and inferior mesenteric back-bleeding can be heavy and continue after the main clamps are on. Controlling it from inside avoids dissection behind the aneurysm.
how: Open the sac longitudinally to the right of the inferior mesenteric artery, and remove thrombus quickly with cell salvage running.
Oversew bleeding lumbar arteries from inside the sac with figure-of-eight sutures.
Control the inferior mesenteric artery from inside, preserving it for reimplantation if back-bleeding is poor and the colon looks at risk.
Place balloon catheters into the iliac orifices if the iliac clamps are not yet on.
structuresAtRisk: Iliac veins behind the iliac orifices
pitfalls: Opening the sac before proximal control is secure.
Ligating the inferior mesenteric artery without assessing colonic perfusion.

step.raaa.graft.title: Graft anastomoses
step.raaa.graft.why: The proximal anastomosis bears the full arterial pressure and is where most bleeding happens. A tube graft is faster than a bifurcated one and is used whenever the iliacs allow.
how: Choose a tube graft if the iliac arteries are not aneurysmal; a bifurcated graft if they are.
Perform the proximal anastomosis with a continuous monofilament suture taking full-thickness bites of the neck, with pledgets if the wall is friable.
Test the proximal anastomosis by moving the clamp onto the graft, then perform the distal anastomosis.
Close the aneurysm sac over the graft to separate it from the duodenum.
pitfalls: Shallow bites on a thin neck that pull through when flow returns.
Leaving the graft in contact with the duodenum, risking a later aorto-enteric fistula.

step.raaa.damage-control.title: Damage control and temporary abdominal closure
step.raaa.damage-control.why: After rupture, the bowel and retroperitoneum swell and the patient is often cold, acidotic and coagulopathic. Forcing the abdomen closed causes compartment syndrome; packing and leaving it open is often the safer operation.
how: If the patient is coagulopathic, cold or acidotic, pack the areas of diffuse bleeding and stop operating.
If the fascia cannot be closed without tension, or the airway pressure rises on closure, use a temporary abdominal closure such as negative pressure.
Return to critical care to warm, correct clotting and resuscitate; plan a return to theatre for pack removal and closure.
Record the number of packs, the clamp times and the plan in the operation note.
pitfalls: Closing the abdomen because it feels like finishing the operation.
